backups.name: North Ridge
gear: 30m rope (short rope for a crux move and/or rappel)
A few slings/webbing for a handline or short rap anchor
hazards: The full traverse from Needle Peak to Bonanza Peak crosses two glaciers and multiple rock towers requiring rappels to bypass
No established bail points exist once past Needle Peak onto the Anonymity Towers–Dark Peak ridge
backups.overview: Needle Peak's North Ridge is the peak's one well-documented technical line, climbed in a single push as the opening stage of a two-day, multi-summit traverse (Needle Peak → Anonymity Towers → Dark Peak → Bonanza Peak) that produced the first ascent of Bonanza Peak's Northwest Ridge.
backups.beta: On August 19, 2006, Blake Herrington and Tim Halder left the Agnes Creek Trail at Swamp Creek and climbed Needle Peak via its North Ridge, then continued along the connecting ridgeline, making the first ascents of the North and South Anonymity Towers, before climbing the Dark Glacier to a bivouac atop Dark Peak. The next day they continued the ridge crest to Bonanza Peak's west and main summits. The overall linkup was rated Grade V, 5.8, and described as 'wild and highly variable in quality' along the crest; the source account does not break the grade, pitch count, or length out separately for the Needle Peak segment alone.
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
obj_haz: Loose, quality-variable alpine rock along the connecting ridge crest
No safe retreat once committed past Needle Peak toward the Anonymity Towers/Dark Peak
Glacier travel on the Dark Glacier and Mary Greene Glacier requiring crevasse-rescue readiness
backups.detailed_rack: A 30m rope and a few slings cover a crux move or short rappel; ice axe for early-season snow on the Swamp Creek basin approach.
pro_tips: Approach via Stehekin and the Agnes Creek Trail, leaving the trail at Swamp Creek to reach Needle Peak's north side

The first-ascent party climbed with minimal bivouac gear (belay jackets and a small tarp instead of a tent/sleeping bags) to move fast over the terrain — plan gear accordingly for an intentionally light, fast style
watch_out: Retreat is very difficult beyond Needle Peak — the first-ascent party noted this 'would not be a good route to begin during unsettled weather'
Rock quality on the ridge crest is described in the account on record as 'wild and highly variable in quality'
backups.best_season: The only documented ascent (August 19–20, 2006) was in mid-to-late summer, consistent with typical North Cascades high-alpine climbing season; the route crosses the Dark Glacier, so late-season timing affects crevasse/moat conditions.
backups.approach: From Stehekin (reached only by passenger boat or floatplane up Lake Chelan — no road access), follow the Agnes Creek Trail upstream and leave the maintained trail at Swamp Creek to travel cross-country onto Needle Peak's north side and gain the North Ridge.
backups.bail: The connecting ridge beyond Needle Peak offers no easy escape — per the first-ascent account, retreating from anywhere along the Anonymity Towers–Dark Peak–Bonanza ridge means retracing the entire traverse, so parties should only commit to this line in settled weather.
backups.itinerary: Day 1: hike from Stehekin via the Agnes Creek Trail to Swamp Creek, climb Needle Peak's North Ridge, continue over the North and South Anonymity Towers, climb the Dark Glacier, and bivouac atop Dark Peak. Day 2: continue the connecting ridge crest to Bonanza Peak's west summit and then the main summit, descending via the Mary Greene Glacier.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
bivy.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

bivy.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
bivy.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
bivy.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

bivy.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
bivy.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
bivy.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

backups.name: South Route
gear: Light rope (~30m) and a few slings for the crux notch/downclimb
Rock shoes or sticky-soled approach shoes for the polished slab and summit moves
Bear canister or a food-hanging kit (a canister is not required at the camps on this route, but food must be hung or stored in a bear-resistant container)
hazards: Loose, 'wobbly' rock and an eroded, polished slab low on the route
Significant exposure at the north-ridge crux (7,300-7,400 ft) with an airy notch downclimb
Old, unvetted rappel webbing left in place at the crux by previous parties — inspect or back it up before trusting it
Wasp nests reported in the approach brush and lower slopes, especially late summer
Fully unmaintained route beyond Swamp Creek Camp — bushwhacking, deadfall, and route-finding required
No cell coverage; remote, rarely-visited peak with long evacuation times
backups.overview: A slender granite spire in the North Cascades backcountry above Stehekin, standing just west of Mount Lyall and linked south to Dark Peak by the jagged, largely unclimbed Anonymity Towers ridge. The peak is not in the Entiat Mountains as earlier described — it rises above the Agnes Creek/Swamp Creek drainage on the west side of Lake Chelan, reached only via the roadless village of Stehekin and the Pacific Crest Trail. It is a rarely-visited, essentially unmaintained scramble/low-5th-class objective, known mainly from a handful of independent trip reports rather than any published description.
backups.beta: Needle Peak sees very few ascents. The standard (and only reported) line leaves the unmaintained Swamp Creek Trail around 3,200 ft, climbs a steep brushy slope to gain the peak's long north ridge near 7,300–7,400 ft, then route-finds through west-facing gullies and krummholz along the ridge before a narrow, choss-filled Class 3 gully leads through stacked boulders to the summit.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before committing to the 7,300 ft crux band — descending the loose, exposed north ridge terrain in the dark is inadvisable, and the remote approach means self-rescue is the default.
backups.permit: NPS wilderness/backcountry permit required for overnight camping in the North Cascades NP/Lake Chelan NRA portion of the approach ($10/person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee); free, self-issued permit once past the wilderness boundary into the Glacier Peak Wilderness (USFS) near Swamp Creek and the peak itself.
backups.comms: No cell coverage anywhere along the approach or on the route (per on-file hazards and emergency notes); carry a satellite messenger (e.g. Garmin inReach/Zoleo) — self-rescue is the default given the remote, boat-only access.
backups.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

waypoints.name: High Bridge PCT/Agnes Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of the Stehekin Valley shuttle road; PCT crosses High Bridge here, southbound tread starts about a quarter-mile up the road toward Agnes Creek.
waypoints.directions: There is no road connection to this trailhead from outside the valley: reach Stehekin by the Lake Chelan ferry or floatplane, then take the Stehekin Valley Road or the NPS shuttle about eleven miles up-valley to the bridge. Plan the whole trip around the boat and shuttle timetable, because missing the last run means an extra night.

waypoints.name: Fivemile Camp (Agnes Creek)
waypoints.note: First established creekside camp on the PCT south of High Bridge; reliable water from Agnes Creek.
waypoints.directions: Walk a few hundred yards up the road from the bridge to pick up the PCT heading south, then follow it into the Agnes Creek valley. The tread is well graded and gains only a few hundred feet through old-growth forest, with the gorge and its cascades off to the side for much of the way.

waypoints.name: Swamp Creek Camp
waypoints.note: PCT camp at the Swamp Creek fork; jumping-off point for the unmaintained boot path toward Needle Peak's north ridge.
waypoints.directions: Keep heading south on the PCT for roughly another three miles of easy valley walking to the fork where Swamp Creek comes in. The peak shows itself up-valley along this stretch. Most parties treat this as an overnight approach rather than pushing straight through from the boat.

waypoints.name: Boot path departure at 3,200 ft
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Swamp Creek trail here onto a steep, brushy, unmarked boot path climbing toward the north ridge crest.
waypoints.directions: From camp pick up the unmaintained trail up the Swamp Creek drainage; expect blowdown, eroded tread and heavy brush, plus a crossing of Swamp Creek itself on a large downed log. Wasps are a recurring nuisance in this overgrown section. The path is left behind at about 3,200 ft, below the north ridge.

waypoints.name: Polished slab gully, ~5,000 ft
waypoints.note: Slick, polished slab in the gully; parties bypass west through rock with a tree belay to gain about 200 ft.
waypoints.directions: Climb straight up the steep, brushy hillside toward the ridge, roughly 1,800 ft of gain with no tread, on vegetation, dirt and small steps of rock. Higher up the ground funnels into the gully system. The slab at its head is the first place the route stops being a walk.

waypoints.name: Ridgeline camp above 5,400 ft
waypoints.note: Flat ground near the ridge crest with the first clear view of Needle Peak; no water on site, must be hauled up from below.
waypoints.directions: Do not force the polished slab directly. The usual line escapes west through the taller rock, and parties belay off a tree for roughly 200 ft to regain the top of the gully, so carry a rope for this leg. Above it the angle eases onto the crest and flat ground appears.

waypoints.name: Crux notch, 7,300-7,400 ft
waypoints.note: Exposed Class 4/5.0 notch with krummholz for holds and wobbly boulders on the ridge above; this is the section that is downclimbed or rappelled on descent.
waypoints.directions: From the camp the ridge steepens into dense krummholz and sloping slabs beneath the sheer north face; stay west of the crest and weave through the cliff bands rather than trying the face. Taking the rib immediately west of the gully gives better holds, and the two lines merge after about 600 ft of gain. Exposure above the talus field is serious through here and blocks are loose — this is Class 4 with a 5.0 move at the notch, not a walk-up.

waypoints.name: Needle Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit; final approach is a narrow gully with overhanging rock below the top.
waypoints.directions: Step across the notch onto the summit ridge and follow ledges just below the crest on its east side. The crest itself overhangs and is stacked with wobbly rock near the top, so the last stretch drops into a narrow gully before topping out. Study this section on the way up, because it is the piece you have to reverse or rappel coming down.

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is required — every documented ascent is an unroped scramble. Bring a helmet for the loose rock in the upper cliff bands and gully, trekking poles for the brushy lower approach, and a light ice axe if snow lingers in the gullies early in the season.
what_to_bring: NPS wilderness permit (reserved or self-issued) for the park/NRA portion of the approach
Overnight camping gear for Swamp Creek Camp
Extra water — camp sits well below the summit with no reliable water higher up
Insect repellent (wasp activity reported on the approach)
Topo map/GPS track — the route is unmarked and unmaintained beyond Swamp Creek Camp
Satellite messenger — no cell coverage in the valley or on route
pro_tips: Break the long approach into two days by camping at Swamp Creek Camp before the climb
Inspect or back up the old webbing at the crux notch before weighting it — its age and condition are unknown
Target August once the 5,000 ft slab gully and upper snow patches have melted out
Check the ferry/shuttle schedule and any active wildfire closures for Stehekin before committing to a trip
watch_out: The crux notch downclimb near the summit has committing exposure — many parties choose to rope up here
The ~5,000 ft slab gully gets slick when wet or in early season with residual snow/ice
Route-finding through the 7,300-7,400 ft cliff bands is the reported crux — parties have wandered into harder terrain trying to stay too close to the ridge crest
backups.pro_needs: Minimal rack — a light rope plus a few slings/small pieces to back up or replace the crux notch anchor; this is a scramble with a short technical crux, not a pitched rock climb.
backups.best_season: August into early September is most reliable: the approach's 5,000 ft slab gully and the north-facing terrain below the crux often still hold snow into July, and the route is essentially unmaintained beyond Swamp Creek Camp, so expect brush and deadfall regardless of timing. Wasp nests in the approach brush become more of an issue by late summer.
backups.approach: Needle Peak is only reachable by boat or floatplane: ride the Lady of the Lake ferry (or a Chelan Airways floatplane) up 50-mile-long Lake Chelan from the town of Chelan to Stehekin Landing — there is no road access from the outside world. From Stehekin Landing, take the Stehekin Valley Road (or the NPS shuttle) about 11 miles up-valley to High Bridge, where the road crosses the Stehekin River and the Pacific Crest Trail comes down off Cottonwood Camp and continues south as the Agnes Creek Trail. Follow the PCT/Agnes Creek Trail (National Park Service-maintained, gentle grade through old-growth forest along Agnes Creek) roughly 8-9 miles south to Swamp Creek Camp (about 2,800 ft), a designated PCT camp and the standard base for the peak — most parties treat this as an overnight approach rather than a single push. From camp, leave the PCT and pick up the unmaintained Swamp Creek Trail heading north/northeast up the Swamp Creek drainage; expect heavy blowdown, erosion, and brush-choked tread that has seen little maintenance in years. Cross Swamp Creek itself on a large fallen log around 3,600 ft (a small waterfall near 3,500 ft and a side stream joining Swamp Creek near 5,200 ft are the last reliable water before the upper mountain, though both can thin out late season). Around 3,200 ft, below Needle's north/south ridge system, most parties leave the Swamp Creek Trail proper and climb a steep, brushy slope directly toward the peak, working through dense foliage and sloping slabs. Near 5,000 ft a polished, slick slab gully is best avoided by staying west through a band of rocks; above that the line continues over talus and (even in summer) lingering snow, aiming for the prominent 7,300 ft notch on Needle's north side, below the steep north ridge and face rising above Swamp Creek, that gives the route its character. Watch for wobbly, loose-grained blocks on the upper talus and near the notch, wasp nests in the brush lower down, and route-finding difficulty in the unmaintained brush sections — this is a full mountaineering day (or two) from camp, not a casual scramble.
backups.descent_text: Descend the same north-ridge line used on ascent: from the summit, reverse the class 3 gully above the notch (some parties find an alternate exposed gully slightly east of the ascent line 'looks manageable from above' but funnels into the same terrain) and downclimb to the crux 7,300-7,400 ft notch. This notch is the one place on the route where parties differ — many downclimb it unroped on adequate but exposed hand/footholds, while others back off with a single rappel of roughly 30 m/100 ft. There is no fixed or bolted rappel station here: any anchor is a natural one (slung block, horn, or krummholz/tree) built by the descending party, and old rappel webbing/cord has been reported at the notch by multiple parties of unclear age and origin — treat any found tat as unverified and back it up or replace it rather than trusting it outright. Below the notch, work back down through the talus and snow, staying on the west side of the cliff bands to avoid the steeper, more exposed rock, then pick back through the polished slab gully near 5,000 ft (stemming with the help of trees rooted in the cracks helps on the slicker sections) and down the brushy slope to rejoin the unmaintained Swamp Creek Trail around 3,200 ft. Follow Swamp Creek Trail back down to Swamp Creek Camp on the PCT (re-crossing Swamp Creek on the same log around 3,600 ft), then retrace the Agnes Creek Trail/PCT roughly 8-9 miles to High Bridge and the Stehekin Valley Road for the shuttle or walk back to Stehekin Landing and the ferry. No technical descent gear beyond a single rope/rack for the optional notch rappel is needed; the rest is a sustained, loose, brushy class 2-3 walk-down with real route-finding demands.
backups.bail: The clearest bail-out point is below the 7,300-7,400 ft cliff-band crux, before committing to the notch downclimb; retreat from there simply reverses the ascent line back to Swamp Creek Camp.

itinerary.cal: Requires a North Cascades NP backcountry camping permit for the Swamp Creek zone, and access depends on the Stehekin ferry/shuttle and the seasonal High Bridge shuttle (roughly June-Sept); best conditions are mid-July through September once the approach trail and gully snow have melted out.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day, ~24-mile round-trip backpack via ferry/shuttle to High Bridge and the Agnes Creek/Swamp Creek Trail, built around one long summit day that gains roughly 5,100 ft on exposed Class 3-4 terrain above camp.

access.fees: Lady of the Lake ferry from Chelan (fares vary by boat/season) or floatplane charter to reach Stehekin; Stehekin shuttle bus to High Bridge is about $10/adult, $5/child one-way. No separate climbing fee.
access.rules: Standard NPS wilderness regulations apply in the park/NRA portion (permit and, where applicable, designated-site camping, bear canister recommended); standard Leave No Trace and USFS wilderness group-size limits apply once past the wilderness boundary.
access.permit: An NPS wilderness/backcountry permit is required for any overnight camping within the North Cascades National Park Complex boundary (the lower Agnes Creek Trail corridor) — $10/person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee if booked in advance via recreation.gov, or self-issued at the Stehekin Ranger Station when the Wilderness Information Center is unstaffed. Once across into the Glacier Peak Wilderness (USFS) near Swamp Creek, permits are free, self-issued trailhead registers.
access.closures: Stehekin Valley Road and the village have faced wildfire evacuation closures in recent fire seasons (e.g., the 2024 Pioneer Fire) — check NPS and Chelan County alerts before a trip. Sisi Fire: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest closure order 06-17-02-2026-35 (Sisi Fire), in effect August 22 through December 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, closes the Pacific Crest Trail (Trail 2000) along Agnes Creek on the Chelan Ranger District, along with Agnes Creek Trail 1272, Agnes Gorge Trail 1281 and Swamp Creek Trail 1242. North Cascades National Park's Sisi Fire closures (its fire-closure list, updated September 14, 2026, gives no end date) also close the Pacific Crest Trail from the park boundary down to High Bridge and on to Bridge Creek Camp, the High Bridge area, and the Stehekin Valley Road from Stehekin Valley Ranch to High Bridge. This approach cannot be used while these closures stand. Chelan Ranger District: (509) 682-4900. North Cascades National Park: (360) 854-7200.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Complex / Lake Chelan National Recreation Area (NPS) covers the Stehekin–High Bridge–lower Agnes Creek corridor; the route transitions into the Glacier Peak Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chelan Ranger District) for the Swamp Creek approach and the peak itself.
access.passRequired: None for day use of the National Forest portion; an NPS wilderness camping permit (see Permit) is required for overnight stays within the Park/NRA portion.

overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or arrange it with the park the day before you travel; there is no permit office or cell service in Stehekin.

road.name: Stehekin Valley Road (boat landing to High Bridge)
road.status: Not connected to any outside highway — Stehekin is accessible only by boat, floatplane, or trail. Within the valley, the road is a local shuttle/bike route from the boat landing to High Bridge (~11 mi). North Cascades National Park has closed the Stehekin Valley Road from Stehekin Valley Ranch to High Bridge, and the High Bridge area, for the Sisi Fire (park fire-closure list updated September 14, 2026; no end date given).
road.driveNote: Reach Stehekin via the Lady of the Lake ferry from Chelan or by floatplane charter; from the boat landing, ride the Stehekin shuttle bus (~$10 adult one-way) or bike/walk the valley road to the High Bridge trailhead.
road.seasonalGate: Ferry and shuttle run year-round on a reduced winter schedule; the trail beyond High Bridge is typically snow-free from July into October.

climate.fall: Early snow can arrive by mid-to-late September at this elevation, and shortening days plus the boat/shuttle schedule compress the usable window.
climate.spring: Heavy lingering snow into June keeps the off-trail gullies avalanche-prone and makes the unmaintained Swamp Creek Trail hard to follow.
climate.summer: Late July through September offers the most reliable dry, snow-free scrambling window (as in the documented September 2023 ascent).
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible — Stehekin itself is snowed in and boat/floatplane service is reduced; no winter ascents are documented.
climate.typical: Dry, warm summer days at elevation with cold nights; afternoon thunderstorms are possible July-August. North-facing terrain below the crux holds snow later into summer than typical south-facing Cascades approaches.

bySeason.fall: A narrow window in early-to-mid September is possible before fall snow returns; days shorten quickly and access logistics (ferry schedule) get tighter.
bySeason.spring: Generally not viable — snow lingers in the approach gullies and on the crux terrain well into early summer.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the best window, though early-summer parties report lingering snow in the 5,000 ft slab gully and upper gullies into July.
bySeason.winter: Not a recognized route — roadless Stehekin access, avalanche exposure on the approach, and the technical crux make a winter ascent impractical for typical parties.

climate.forecastZone: Approximately NWS Zone WAZ522, "Upper Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest" (forecast.weather.gov)

emergency.notes: Stehekin is roadless; medical evacuation is typically by NPS/private boat down-lake or by helicopter staged out of Brewster, WA (~30 min flight time). Call the North Cascades NPS Wilderness Information Center, (360) 854-7245, for trip planning or to help coordinate backcountry rescue.
emergency.rangerStation: NPS Golden West Visitor Center / Stehekin Ranger Station (Stehekin) for the park/NRA portion; Chelan Ranger District office, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, (509) 682-4900, for the Glacier Peak Wilderness portion.
emergency.nearestHospital: Lake Chelan Health (Lake Chelan Community Hospital), Chelan, WA — roughly 50 lake-miles from Stehekin by boat; there is no road connection.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911, routed to Chelan County Sheriff's Office — no cell coverage in the Stehekin valley or on route, so plan a communication device (satellite messenger) in advance.

crowds.peakTraffic: Rarely climbed; the ~24-mile round trip from High Bridge via the PCT (with a multi-day approach through Swamp Creek/Agnes Creek country) strongly limits day-trip and casual traffic to essentially none
crowds.estimatePerSeason: unknown - low-traffic, plausibly single-digit to low-double-digit parties per season given the remote, multi-day wilderness approach

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong backcountry fitness - the approach alone (High Bridge via PCT to a Swamp Creek-area base camp) is roughly 24 miles round trip with substantial elevation gain, typically broken into a multi-day trip rather than a single push
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day pack weight (shelter, food, water treatment for a multi-day wilderness approach) for at least the approach and camp portion, dropping to a light summit-day pack for the scramble itself

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long - a multi-day wilderness approach (roughly 24 miles round trip from High Bridge via the PCT and Swamp Creek to the north ridge), not a single-day car-to-summit outing

comfort with exposure at the narrow, exposed summit step
wilderness navigation (off-trail route-finding above the basins, no maintained summit trail)
multi-day backcountry travel / camp skills for the long approach
loose rock (choss) management and careful foot/handhold testing

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through September, with August as the core optimal month

July.reason: Early July can still hold lingering snow on the approach and in the summit basins; conditions generally firm up and become favorable only by late July

August.reason: Peak dry-season window - most consistent snow-free talus/rock conditions and stable weather for the exposed summit step

September.reason: Generally still climbable with dry rock, but shorter daylight and higher chance of early-season snow or storms late in the month, especially at this long multi-day approach's exposed elevations

weather.typical: East Cascades summer pattern - generally warm and dry with cool nights at elevation, consistent with the Stehekin/Lake Chelan backcountry location
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms/convective buildups are a realistic risk on east-slope Cascades summits in summer, which would compound the loose-rock and exposure hazards near the summit

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Consequential but localized - the primary fall exposure is concentrated at the final summit step, where a slip on loose rock could result in a serious fall; the broader talus approach is lower-consequence but still requires care due to loose rock underfoot

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; NWAC does not issue forecasts during the July-September climbing season, and no NWAC winter zone is specific to this remote Agnes Creek-area summit

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; this is a talus/rock scramble route

backups.rope_type: Optional 30m rope for the 5.0 crux move and/or rappel descent
backups.rope_note: A light 30 m rope and a few slings, for one place: the notch at 7,300-7,400 ft. Many parties downclimb it unroped on adequate but exposed holds and others back off it with a single rappel of about 30 m, and the exposure is committing enough that it is better to have the rope than to decide you want it from above. There is no fixed or bolted station there - any anchor is one you build off a slung block, horn or krummholz - and the old webbing already at the notch is of unknown age, so inspect or back it up before you weight it. Otherwise this is a scramble rather than a pitched climb: no technical rack, a helmet for the loose rock throughout, and sticky-soled shoes for the polished slab.

approach_variants.name: Agnes Creek crest trail to Swamp Creek Camp and the ridge
approach_variants.notes: No road reaches this valley: take the passenger ferry or a floatplane up the lake to the landing, then the valley road or the shuttle up to the bridge at the road end, and plan the whole trip around those timetables. Walk a few hundred yards up the road to pick up the crest trail heading south, then follow well-graded tread through old-growth forest into the Agnes Creek valley past the first creekside camp, and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork — the standard overnight base. The peak shows itself up-valley along that stretch. From camp pick up the unmaintained trail up the Swamp Creek drainage, with blowdown, eroded tread, heavy brush and a crossing of Swamp Creek on a large downed log, and leave it near 3,200 ft below the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends. Snow lingers on the upper talus even in summer.
hazards: The Swamp Creek path is unmaintained and heavily overgrown, with wasps a recurring nuisance in the brush
About 1,800 ft of trackless steep brushy climbing on vegetation, dirt and small rock steps
A slick polished slab at the head of the gully near 5,000 ft, bypassed with a rope and a tree belay
Serious exposure above the talus field and loose, wobbly blocks near the notch and on the summit ridge
No water on the ridge — it has to be carried up from below
The crest overhangs near the top and the last stretch drops into a narrow gully that has to be reversed or rappelled
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE POLISHED SLAB LOW DOWN AND THE BUTTRESS BETWEEN TWO GULLIES HIGHER UP ARE THE TWO PROOFS. Leave the unmaintained drainage path near 3,200 ft, below the ridge, and climb straight up steep brushy hillside with no tread at all — vegetation, dirt and small steps of rock. Around 5,000 ft the ground funnels into a gully whose head is a slick, polished slab; that slab is where the route stops being a walk and is how you know you are in the right drainage. Do not force it. The line escapes west through the taller band of rock, with a tree belay for a couple of hundred feet to regain the top of the gully, so carry a rope for this leg. Above it the angle eases and the first clear view of the peak comes at about 5,400 ft off a mild grass slope. Higher, below the sheer north face, two gullies are separated by a buttress: take the WEST one, or better the rib immediately west of it where the krummholz gives better holds. The east gully looks less steep and is the trap — it goes over cliffs, and its crux is crossing the cliff tops. The two lines merge in the upper basin about 600 ft higher.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
bivy.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

bivy.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
bivy.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
bivy.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

bivy.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
bivy.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
bivy.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

backups.name: Lewis Creek Route
backups.fa: Dr. Harry B. Hinman, Walter Eriksen, and Louis Lesh, July 18, 1915, via Lewis Creek, on their fifth attempt at the peak
backups.aspect: S for the approach and most of the climb; crosses to the N side near the summit
backups.season: Jul-Sep is the standard window; snow and high water can persist into July
gear: light rack (optional, for the exposed summit scramble)
hazards: dense brush (alder, devil's club, salmonberry) on the lower approach
loose rock
difficult route-finding through old clear-cuts and unmaintained climbers' path
exposed class 3 scrambling near the summit block
backups.overview: The Lewis Creek Route is the original 1915 first-ascent line up Gunn Peak, named for the Lewis Creek drainage the FA party used on their approach. It is rated 3rd Class (3 stars) and its modern access is via overgrown logging roads leading to a climbers' trail beginning around 3,200 ft on the ragged, brushy crest north of Barclay Creek — essentially the same corridor used by today's standard (Southeast/Tailgunner Pass) approach. It is climbed far less often than the standard line today and is largely of historical interest; expect an unmaintained, easy-to-lose path.
backups.beta: Not a maintained trail — a rough, easily-lost climbers' path that gains roughly 4,000-4,900 ft over 5.5-7.5 miles round trip depending on the exact line and any side trips (figures vary across sources). Expect steep muddy/slick forest low down, a brushy cliff-and-waterfall traverse, alpine meadows and boulder fields higher up, and a loose, narrow gully/ledge crux just below the summit. Most parties treat it as a long single day (7-10 hours) or descend via the same route.
backups.turnaround: This is a long, remote, easily-lost scramble with a documented history of search-and-rescue incidents and an exposed, unprotected ledge crux near the summit. Set a firm turnaround time that accounts for round-trip estimates of 7-10+ hours, and do not commit to the summit ledge traverse in wet, icy, or low-visibility conditions.
backups.rappels: None required for most parties in dry conditions; some parties place a short rope-assisted downclimb or rappel through the 'hidden ramp' gully or the summit notch on descent
backups.face: South gully / 'Hidden Ramp' — the standard route
backups.permit: Free self-issue Wild Sky Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
obj_haz: brush and deadfall on the lower approach
creek and waterfall crossing hazard at high early-season water
lingering snow on the shaded north-side ledge into early summer

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is required in normal, dry, snow-free conditions — this is a scrambling route. A helmet is strongly recommended for the loose gully/boulder-field sections due to rockfall (including from other parties).
what_to_bring: map/compass or GPS with a pre-loaded track (route-finding is genuinely difficult)
extra water (no reliable water sources above Barclay Creek)
layers for wind/weather exposure on the upper ridge
headlamp (round trips commonly run 7-10+ hours)
Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking
pro_tips: Find the correct climbers' path early: walk back down the road about 1/4 mile from the Barclay Lake trailhead parking to the old spur/fire-pit turnoff — missing it adds significant bushwhacking.
This route is notorious for faint, hard-to-follow tread; carry or pre-load a GPX track from a recent trip report.
Aim for August-September for the driest, most melted-out conditions on the crux ledge and gully.
watch_out: A narrow, roughly foot-wide ledge with no fall protection traverses the north side of the mountain just below the summit — very dangerous when wet, icy, or snow-covered.
The boulder-field/gully crux below the summit is loose rock and can hold lingering snow into early summer.
The peak has a long history of search-and-rescue callouts; the route is steep, exposed, and easy to get off-route on, especially in poor visibility.
backups.pro_needs: This is essentially unprotected 3rd/4th-class scrambling — a handful of slings for a hip belay or quick running protection at the crux notch and the hidden-ramp gully covers the real 'gear' needs rather than a traditional trad rack.
backups.best_season: July through September (snow-free window); August and September are most reliable for low water and firmer footing on brush-covered slopes.
backups.approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (2,200 ft, end of FR-6024), do not take the maintained Barclay Lake Trail; instead walk back down the access road a short distance to an old spur/climbers' path dropping toward Barclay Creek. Ford Barclay Creek — parties describe essentially two back-to-back crossings, rock-hopping over boulders and deadfall (a small mid-channel island splits the ford), the route's main water hazard and genuinely tricky at high early-season flow. On the far bank, pick up a boot-worn, unsigned climbers' path that starts near the downstream tip of that island and switchbacks relentlessly uphill through second-growth forest — roughly 1,500 vertical feet of steep dirt-and-root tread with few cairns. Around 3,800 ft the path runs into a rock face; go right (don't try to scramble the face itself) and follow a rising traverse beneath cliff bands that crosses a small waterfall/seep with real exposure — arguably the single most consequential stretch of the hike-in. Above this the grade eases through fern-and-alder benches and mixed forest to about 4,400 ft, where the summer line bends left and climbs a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the adjacent Tailgunner couloir (which holds snow late into the season and is a common wrong-turn/avalanche-path hazard). From there, huckleberry-and-heather meadows lead to Tailgunner Pass / the Gunn Lake saddle near 5,400 ft, generally the last reliable water. From the saddle, talus and boulders lead to the base of the class 3-4 'hidden ramp,' where the maintained-feeling climbers' trail effectively ends and the technical scramble route begins. Total gain from trailhead to summit is on the order of 4,600+ ft over only a few miles, almost all of it steep, and the tread is faint enough in several places (especially the final approach to the ramp) that GPS track-following is genuinely useful, not just a nicety.
backups.descent_text: Descent retraces the ascent line — there is no separate descent trail or established walk-off. The crux is reversing the 'hidden ramp' below the summit block: most parties downclimb this exposed class 3-4 terrain facing in, checking GPS/landmarks to confirm the correct ledge or gully, but parties note a fixed or improvised rappel anchor (webbing/tat around a horn or chockstone — not bolted) at the top of the trickiest scramble move on the ramp, and it's common for parties to make one short, single-strand rappel there (well under 30 m/one rope length) rather than downclimb it, particularly if the rock is wet or there's residual snow. Below the ramp, downclimb talus and heather back to Tailgunner Pass/Gunn Lake saddle, then reverse the brushy cliff-band weakness and the exposed traverse beneath the cliff bands past the waterfall/seep — use extra caution here if wet. From about 3,800 ft, descend the same steep, faint climbers' trail back down through the forest to Barclay Creek, re-ford it, and rejoin the spur road back to the Barclay Lake Trailhead. Route-finding is the dominant descent hazard on this peak — parties often mention needing to double-check GPS to find the correct gully/ledge off the ramp and to avoid dropping into the Tailgunner couloir by mistake — so most parties treat the one short rappel (or careful downclimb) on the hidden ramp as the only technical rope-work required, with everything else being steep hiking/scrambling.
backups.bail: There is no established bail-out short of retreating the way you came; the crux gully/ledge section can be down-climbed by parties comfortable with Class 3-4 exposure. Turn back before committing to the exposed north-side ledge traverse if it is wet, snow-covered, or icy.

pitch_detail.notes: Barclay Lake TH down the road ~1/4 mi to old spur/fire-pit turnoff, then two crossings of Barclay Creek.
Steep forest climb, muddy transitioning to dry dirt, for roughly the first mile.
Steep, trail-less section on slick, dirt-covered rock; hands needed.
Traverse beneath a cliff band, drop to and pass a small waterfall (branch-assisted squeeze), climb out on rockier ground.
Berry meadows, Baring Mountain viewpoint, overgrown brush, up to the alpine high point between Wing, Tailgunner and Gunn peaks.
Drop and traverse around a subsidiary bump on a faint path along its southern side.
Steep boulder field to a hidden gully (or an alternate, more-exposed rock scramble beside it); the technical crux of the route.

itinerary.cal: Best attempted July-September once snow clears the north-facing basin and brush is driest; this off-trail line has minimal beta, so treat it as an expedition-style day requiring strong navigation skills.

days.note: This is the historic 1915 first-ascent line up the Lewis Creek drainage on the peak's north/west side, distinct from (and far less traveled than) the now-standard Barclay Lake climbers' trail. Expect real bushwhacking low down, then open talus/basin travel higher, with essentially no cairns, flagging, or boot path to follow — budget extra time for navigation.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Summer-only, roughly July through September, with August-September commonly cited as optimal once high water on stream crossings has subsided and any lingering snow/ice on the crux summit ledge has melted out.

July.reason: Within the standard summer window, though the crux narrow summit ledge may still carry snow/ice in some years.

August.reason: One late-July ascent during an unusually hot year found the crux ledge fully melted out and straightforward; low water favors the Barclay Creek and waterfall crossings.

September.reason: Cited alongside August as a favorable late-season window with low water and a melted-out summit ledge.

weather.typical: Standard Central Cascades summer pattern -- afternoon cloud buildup can obscure the summit even in July; a weekday/early start is commonly recommended to beat both weather and any parking congestion at the Barclay Lake trailhead.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: The class 3 (locally 'class 3/4') summit block and especially a foot-wide exposed ledge on the north side are repeatedly singled out as high-consequence -- 'little more than a foot wide,' 'no safety net' -- and are worse when wet, snowy, or icy; numerous search and rescue missions have been reported on this route.

avalanche.zone: N/A -- no dedicated avalanche-zone documentation found; the operative winter/spring hazard described by sources is technical difficulty and fall/slip risk from snow/ice on rock rather than slide risk.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek and Tailgunner Pass to the hidden ramp
approach_variants.notes: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, walk back down the access road a short way to an old spur dropping toward Barclay Creek and ford it — effectively two back-to-back crossings over boulders and deadfall, split by a small mid-channel island, and genuinely tricky at early-season flow. An unsigned boot-worn path starts near the downstream tip of that island and switchbacks relentlessly up about 1,500 vertical feet of dirt and root. Near 3,800 ft it runs into a rock face: go right and take the rising traverse beneath the cliff bands, which crosses a waterfall seep with real exposure. Above that the grade eases through fern and alder benches to about 4,400 ft, where the summer line bends left through a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the adjacent couloir, and meadows lead to the pass and Gunn Lake saddle near 5,400 ft.
hazards: Two creek crossings that are serious at high flow
An exposed traverse beneath cliff bands past a waterfall seep
Loose rock and exposure on the ramp and the summit ledges
Steep snow on the north side of the summit notch into early summer
Faint tread that is easy to lose in both directions
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts at the hidden ramp, and it earns the name — from below it does not look like a way through. Drop off the pass into the basin and cross large talus blocks toward the peak's northern side. The ramp is the drippy, uninviting weakness angling up and to the RIGHT through a lower cliff band; it looks harder and wetter than it is. The line is not the wet centre but the steep face on its right-hand edge, which gives clean and enjoyable class 3 up to trees and a hanging snowfield above. If nothing in the cliff band in front of you looks like it goes at all, you are probably still below the ramp rather than at it. Above the snowfield the route continues to a tiny notch immediately east of the summit — the point where a June attempt commonly ends, because the north face beyond holds steep snow. Squirm through the notch onto the north side and the remaining ground is a traverse of exposed heather ledges and snowpatches, then a short class 3 scramble to the top. The standing error on this mountain is dropping into the adjacent couloir by mistake, on the way up or on the way down.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

backups.overview: Gunn Peak is an extraordinarily prominent summit above the Sultan Basin and Skykomish valley — the highest point in the Wild Sky Wilderness and the 29th-most prominent peak in Washington, its 3,600-plus feet of prominence making it a coveted objective. First climbed July 18, 1915 by Dr. Harry B. Hinman, Walter Eriksen, and Louis Lesh. The standard route climbs from Barclay Lake Trailhead over Tailgunner Pass into Gunn Basin, then up the southwest corner of the summit block via a hidden, often-wet Class 3 ramp through a lower cliff band (the 'hidden ramp'), squeezing through a notch east of the true summit to exposed heather ledges on the north side leading to the top. Few parties climb it each year, largely due to the brushy, easy-to-lose approach and short but serious summit-block exposure; many combine it with neighboring Tailgunner Peak.
backups.beta: Serious alpine scramble requiring climbing experience and high mountain skills. Follows overgrown logging roads and climbers' trails from Barclay Lake, ascending steeply through forest to boulder field approach. Technical crux is an exposed class 3-4 hidden ramp with loose rock and significant exposure. A narrow ledge on north side of summit requires careful foot placement, especially in wet or icy conditions. Multiple search and rescue incidents have occurred on this peak.
backups.turnaround: Start descent by 3-4 PM at latest to ensure full daylight return to trailhead. Be especially conservative in autumn (shorter days) and spring (weather instability).
backups.rock_grade: Class 2-4 scrambling, with exposed class 3-4 sections on the hidden-ramp-equivalent step and the summit block
backups.rappels: A short rappel is sometimes placed over the steepest scramble step on descent; otherwise the route is climbed unroped with occasional running belays
backups.face: South Face / East Ridge via Tailgunner Pass and Gunn Point
backups.permit: Free self-issue Wild Sky Wilderness permit or trailhead registration; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
backups.comms: Cell phone service unreliable or absent in Barclay Lake area and Wild Sky Wilderness. Download offline topographic maps (Gaia GPS, Caltopo, or similar) before departing. Carry satellite messenger or personal locator beacon (PLB) if possible, as multiple search and rescue operations conducted on this peak.
backups.descent: Reverse the ascent: downclimb the exposed heather ledges and the 'hidden ramp' back through the notch (some parties place a hand-line or short rappel on the ramp if wet or for less-experienced members), then re-cross Gunn Basin, back over Tailgunner Pass, and down the brushy climbers' path to the Barclay Creek log jam and trailhead.
obj_haz: brush and deadfall on the lower approach
steep, hard snowpatches on the north-facing traverse into midsummer
long, remote approach via Tailgunner Pass

waypoints.name: Barclay Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue day-use fee ($5) or Northwest Forest Pass at the kiosk; vault toilet on site, no potable water; walk back down the access road ~0.25 mi to find the old forest road turnoff.
waypoints.directions: Leave US 2 at Baring and follow FS Road 6024 to its end at the Barclay Lake trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required here, or pay the $5 self-issue day-use fee at the kiosk. There is a vault toilet at the lot but no potable water, so arrive with what you need. Note that this route does not start on the Barclay Lake trail — you walk back down the access road about a quarter mile to an old gated spur road, and parties who already know the line often park at that spur start rather than driving on to the main lot.

waypoints.name: Barclay Creek log jam crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the first log jam, then immediately turn left and follow the south shore of the smaller creek branch on a flagged path for ~50 yards rather than crossing the tempting second log jam, which leads to a trail that fades out.

waypoints.name: Cliff-band brush weakness (leaves couloir line)
waypoints.note: Around 3,800-4,400 ft the climbers' path bends right off the rock face and pushes up a brushy weakness in the cliff band into ferns, alders, then huckleberry-heather meadows dotted with light gray rock.

waypoints.name: Ramp/chockstone crux
waypoints.note: A short (~10 ft) Class 3-4 ramp past a cliff band; the gully line has a chockstone move nearing low Class 5, the climbers'-right alternative avoids it but feels more exposed.

waypoints.name: The notch
waypoints.note: Boulder-hop up from the hidden bench to an opening on the left revealing a notch to hop through onto the upper south face; this is the key navigational landmark referenced on both ascent and descent.

waypoints.name: Exposed upper south face traverse
waypoints.note: Cross two remnant snowpatches and an exposed heather/rock ledge below a smooth granite wall with a steep drop-off; parties report using a handline here and carrying an axe into early July.

waypoints.name: Gunn Peak summit
waypoints.note: Final Class 3 boulder scramble to the true summit; sweeping views over the Wild Sky Wilderness toward Monte Cristo and the Skykomish valley.

backups.detailed_rack: No rock protection needed as this is a scramble, not a rock climbing route. However, carry 1-2 runners/slings and carabiners if planning to use rappel station above hidden ramp section. A 30 m rope is optional but recommended for groups with inexperienced members, as a handline or for the one short rappel at the hidden ramp.

pro_tips: The exposed summit ramp becomes dangerous when wet — avoid climbing it during or right after rain.
Many parties link Gunn Peak with neighboring Tailgunner Peak via the connecting ridge and a small tarn near Tailgunner Pass.
The climbers' path beyond the old logging road is unmaintained and easy to lose; a GPS track or prior route beta is strongly recommended.
backups.pro_needs: No technical protection required for ascent (scramble), but some parties install slings and anchors at hidden ramp crux to facilitate safe descent via rappel. If descending by rappel, ensure anchor integrity before committing weight.
backups.best_season: Late July through September for reliable snow-free conditions; August is generally the most reliable month (lower creek levels, drier brush and ramp). An early-season variant exists via the snow-filled Tailgunner Couloir but requires different gear/skills.
backups.approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,200 ft, end of FS Rd 6024 out of Baring) do not follow the maintained Barclay Lake Trail #1055; instead walk back down the access road roughly a quarter mile and pick up the old, deactivated Barclay Creek spur road (parties who know the route often park directly at the spur's gated start rather than the main Barclay Lake lot). Follow the old roadbed about 100-200 yards to a fire-pit clearing, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden 'Gunn climbers' path.' The path drops to Barclay Creek and crosses via a log-jam/rock-hop near the downstream tip of a small mid-channel island — this ford is the approach's main early-season hazard, since the crossing can run high and slick with spring runoff. On the far bank the boot path swings west then turns north and starts climbing in earnest: about 200 ft of easier grade gives way to sustained, tight switchbacks gaining roughly 1,500 ft through second-growth timber with generally good tree/root holds underfoot but a steep, sometimes loose tread. Around 3,600-3,800 ft the path forks near a band of exposed rock — stay right and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, a known route-finding trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band in partial shade. A usually-dry waterfall ravine is crossed around 4,400 ft (can carry meltwater and be slick in early season). The trail continues switchbacking up brushy, sometimes slide-alder-choked terrain for another ~1,500 ft to gain the ridge crest at roughly 5,400 ft — call it 3-4 hours and about 3,200 ft of gain above the creek crossing for a fit party. From the ridge crest, drop about 100 ft off the crest to skirt a cliff band, then boulder-hop roughly 500 ft up a talus basin to the upper tree benches directly below the peak's south face, which marks the base of the summit scrambling. There is no reliable water above Barclay Creek/the waterfall ravine in late summer, so fill up early. Cairns thin out badly above treeline and the boot path fades in the talus, so route-finding (not technical difficulty) is the main hazard on the upper approach — carrying a GPS track or recent trip-report beta is strongly recommended.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — essentially every accessible way off Gunn's summit block funnels back through the same notch, ledge, and ramp used going up, so this is fundamentally a downclimb/walk-off rather than a rappel route, with one optional short rappel commonly used at the crux. From the summit, downclimb the short class 3 blocks back to the notch between the peak's two summit 'horns,' then reverse the narrow, roughly one-foot-wide dirt/heather ledge traversing the north face — this exposed traverse is the route's crux in both directions and is meaningfully more dangerous descending when wet, icy, or snow-covered; less experienced parties should consider a handline here. Below the ledge, downclimb back through the class 3-4 notch move to the 'hidden ramp,' a roughly 10-ft, near-vertical step in the cliff band with two options: a chockstone-choked gully (near class 5) on the left, or a more exposed class 3-4 line to the right. This ramp is the one spot on the peak where parties commonly rappel instead of downclimbing — parties describe a sling/rappel station left on a horn or chockstone here (a natural anchor, not bolted; inspect and back it up before trusting it), and a single rappel of roughly 15-20 m clears the step, so a 30 m rope doubled is more than sufficient. Confident scramblers frequently downclimb this section unroped instead, and some parties opt to rappel the steeper gully just right of the ramp when it is wet, icy, or holding snow rather than the ramp itself. Below the ramp, re-cross the talus basin, regain the boot path, and climb back up to the ridge crest (~5,400 ft) before dropping down the switchbacking forest trail, re-crossing Barclay Creek at the log jam, and following the old spur road back to the Barclay Lake Trailhead.
backups.bail: Bail points: Lower switchback section (descend back to trailhead at any point); Boulder field (descend back to trailhead by returning to forest edge); Hidden ramp (critical juncture - consider rappel descent or delay to better conditions rather than forcing technical down-climb in poor visibility).

days.note: A relentless, steep, mostly off-trail scramble: cross Barclay Creek, grind up a faint dirt climbers' trail through forest (~2,000-2,500 ft/mile in places), then negotiate talus, the exposed 'hidden ramp,' and a keyhole notch onto a narrow north-side ledge before the final easy scramble to the summit. Most parties treat it as a full daylight outing with an early start.

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate: Pacific weather systems produce strong orographic lift and heavy precipitation on this west-slope Cascades location, with wet, heavy winter/spring snowfall that drives high avalanche danger in the Tailgunner Couloir season.

bySeason.fall: Possible extension into early October in dry years, but shortening daylight and early-season snow are risks.
bySeason.spring: Deep snowpack can cover much of the approach brush (some parties prefer this for easier travel) but the Tailgunner Couloir and upper slopes carry real avalanche hazard.
bySeason.summer: July-September is the practical climbing window; the summit ramp and heather ledges are typically snow-free and driest in August.

emergency.notes: Cell service is unreliable in the Barclay Creek/Gunn Peak drainage; save maps and directions offline. This route has a history of search-and-rescue incidents, largely tied to the exposed summit-block ramp and route-finding on the brushy approach.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek climbers' path — summer line
approach_variants.notes: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, do NOT take the maintained lake trail. Walk back down the access road about a quarter mile and pick up the old deactivated spur road — parties who know it often park at the spur's gated start instead of the main lot. Follow the old roadbed a hundred or two hundred yards to a FIRE-PIT CLEARING, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden climbers' path. It drops to the creek and crosses on a log jam or by rock-hopping near the DOWNSTREAM TIP OF A SMALL MID-CHANNEL ISLAND; this crossing is the main early-season hazard. On the far bank the path swings west, then north, and starts climbing in earnest through sustained tight switchbacks in second-growth timber. Two decision points follow. Around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet the path forks near a BAND OF EXPOSED ROCK — stay RIGHT and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, which is a known trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band. Then around forty-four hundred feet the summer line bends LEFT up a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the couloir, which holds snow late. Huckleberry and heather meadows lead to the saddle at about fifty-four hundred feet, the last reliable water.
approach_variants.season: June to September. Early June parties meet significant lingering snow and heavy brush; late July through August is typically the clearest.
hazards: Steep brush — alder, devil's club and salmonberry — on the lower approach
