approach_variants.baseFinding: From the saddle, drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt a cliff band and boulder-hop up the TALUS FAN toward the upper tree benches directly below the peak's south face. The base of the technical ground is the top of that fan — and the feature you are looking for CANNOT BE SEEN FROM BELOW. A ramp cuts up the face from the top of the talus and only appears once you are underneath it, which is exactly why parties overshoot by continuing up the rockslide. The unmistakable test is the single step at the ramp's foot: a boulder with TWO options off it, a left-hand line past a CHOCKSTONE that takes a steep low-fifth move, and a right-hand line, steeper and more exposed but on solid holds, which is what most parties take. If there is no boulder with a two-way step above it, you are not at the ramp. Negative marker: if you are still grinding up loose rockslide with no ramp cutting off to either side, you have gone past the entry — the ramp is entered FROM the talus, not from the top of it. Higher up, the next landmark is a keyhole notch through the ridge to the north side; if you have not passed the ramp step you will not reach it.

approach_variants.name: Tailgunner couloir — snow-season line
approach_variants.notes: The same start — the spur road, the fire-pit clearing, the creek crossing at the island, and the switchbacks up through the timber. The difference comes at about forty-four hundred feet: instead of bending left into the brushy weakness in the cliff band, the snow-season line continues directly up the couloir to the saddle. This same couloir is a documented WRONG TURN in summer and an avalanche path, so it is only reasonable when it is a continuous snow climb and conditions have been assessed.
approach_variants.season: Late spring, while the couloir holds continuous consolidated snow. Once it starts melting out it becomes the wrong answer and the summer line through the brushy weakness is correct.
hazards: Avalanche hazard — this couloir is an active path and holds snow late
Snow conditions vary hour to hour on it; assess before committing
Everything the summer line carries below the cliff band, including the brushy lower approach and the creek crossing at higher spring flow
The ramp above is harder to protect and downclimb when wet or holding snow, and it is the one place on this peak where parties commonly rappel
approach_variants.baseFinding: The couloir tops out at the same saddle as the summer line, so the base of the climbing is identical: drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt the cliff band, then boulder-hop up the talus fan to the upper tree benches below the south face. The ramp at the top of the fan is invisible until you are under it; identify it by the BOULDER at its foot with a two-way step above — a left-hand chockstone move at low fifth, or a steeper, more exposed line on good holds to the right. Negative marker: if you are still on snow when you expect to be on talus, you have carried on above the saddle into the wrong basin; the couloir delivers you to a saddle, and the talus fan starts on the far side of it.

climbing_route.label: Talus fan below the south face
climbing_route.notes: Ascend the fan of large talus blocks that runs up to the base of the south face directly below the summit. The blocks are big enough to walk on but some shift; the cairns that mark the way lower down have usually thinned to nothing by here, so the line is chosen by eye toward the base of the ramp above.

climbing_route.label: The hidden ramp
climbing_route.notes: The route's crux, and it is short. A ramp cuts up the face from the top of the talus and is not obvious until you are underneath it. The hard part is the single step off the boulder at its foot: the left-hand option passes a chockstone and involves a steep low fifth-class move, while the right-hand option is a steep, exposed Class 3-4 sequence on solid holds and is the line most parties take. Above that step the ramp itself eases. Some parties sling the ramp for a belay or a handline; a short rope is worth carrying even though a confident scrambler will not need it.

climbing_route.label: Upper south face to the high notch
climbing_route.notes: Above the ramp, cross the upper south face — typically over two remnant snow patches that persist well into summer — and scramble to the high notch between the west and east summits. In June, or any heavy snow year, these patches are steep snow immediately above the very exposed north side and turn a scramble into a climb needing axe and crampons; by August they are usually melted out and the section is unremarkable. Judge this from the notch below, not from the trailhead.

climbing_route.label: North-side ledge and summit block
climbing_route.notes: From the notch, traverse north-side heather ledges — easy walking, but with substantial drop below, and parties sometimes leave a handline here for the return. A short Class 3 scramble on the prominent summit block finishes the climb. The descent reverses everything, and the step down off the hidden ramp feels harder than it did going up; plan on downclimbing it carefully or rappelling from a slung block.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.

backups.overview: Guye Peak's steep, sun-exposed West Face rises directly above the Alpental valley and is one of the most visible alpine rock walls from I-90 at Snoqualmie Pass. It holds several moderate multi-pitch lines on generally featured but often dirty and loose Cascade rock, following discontinuous ramp and slab systems up to the summit ridge; the best-known specific line on this face is the Improbable Traverse. A November 2021 rockfall event stripped a large section of rock from the face and buried lower pitches in dirt and debris, changing conditions from older route descriptions.
backups.beta: From Alpental parking, make a rising traverse up talus to the far left (north) side of the west face (note private road access restrictions as of 2021). Ascend a very large ramp that traverses the entire face from north to south. The climbing starts up a steep crack/face (crux) for approximately 30 feet of low 5th class, then transitions to Class 4 for about half a rope length through rocks and alpine trees with exposure. Climbing continues via mixed scrambling and rock sections to the summit. Route involves significant high-consequence scrambling.
backups.turnaround: Because the crux traverse pitch is currently degraded by 2021 rockfall damage and the descent requires downclimbing exposed, loose terrain, turn back if the rock is wet, if daylight is limited, or if any party member is not confident downclimbing loose 5th-class terrain — Cascade afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer and this route has no quick retreat once past the traverse.
backups.rappels: Rappel from a tree anchor on the east side, then a short gully to bypass the true summit (single-rope rap; length depends on tree used)
backups.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, May 15-Oct 31 (available at the trailhead box)
backups.comms: Cell coverage generally reliable at Snoqualmie Pass itself but can be spotty on the peak's north and east sides
backups.descent: Most parties descend via the South Rib/South Gully line or walk off toward the Cave Ridge saddle and back down to the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead; some rappel from fixed anchors near the top of the Improbable Traverse pitch. Loose rock on the descent gullies is a real hazard — keep helmets on until back at the talus.

backups.approach: From the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead (~3,100-3,120 ft, I-90 Exit 52), pick up the unsigned climbers' path that leaves the pavement about 100 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead sign. It fords a small stream almost immediately, then climbs steeply — dirt, roots, loose talus — straight up Guye's southeast flank with no real flat sections. After roughly 1 mile and about 1,000 ft of gain, the boot path breaks into the open at a junction where the right fork heads for Guye Peak/Cave Ridge and the left continues toward Commonwealth Basin and the PCT. Bear right, then make a rising traverse across a large, unstable talus field to the base of the west face — helmet on here, since climber-triggered rockfall is a real hazard on this talus, both from your own party and anyone above. Near the north end of the talus you'll cross a rocky streambed that's often dry by mid-to-late summer (your last realistic water before the climb). From there it's a short scramble up broken rock/slab to the base of the West Face route proper. Total approach is around 1.5 miles and 1,500-2,000 ft of gain, roughly 45 minutes to 1.5 hours depending on conditions and pace.
backups.descent_text: West Face tops out on Guye's south summit (where the route tops out and the register sits; GPS surveys suggest the north summit may be marginally higher) at ~5,169-5,172 ft alongside the middle and north summits, and the descent is a scramble/rappel traverse north along the connecting ridge rather than a reversal of the climbing line. From the south summit, follow the climber's path around the east (right) side of the middle summit to the notch between the south and middle summits. The drop into the gully here is loose, mossy class 3/4 slab; most parties rappel rather than downclimb it. The total rappelling on this route comes to roughly 100 ft, enough that many groups get by with an arm-wrap/hip rappel off a sling rather than a full rap setup, though bringing a rope and device is still the sane default. Important: there is a tree at the top of the gully between the south and middle summits that climbers should specifically NOT rappel from (flagged as unsound/inadvisable in route notes) — use the established sling/anchor lower or to the side instead. Past the middle-summit notch, descend the gully and slabs to the right (east side) to go around the north summit, then scramble up an easy gully to the notch on the north summit's north side. From there, a well-defined scrambler's trail leads down past a small pond, then west (left) back to the Alpental parking lot. Bring a single 30m+ rope and rap device even though the raps are short — anchor tat and rock quality are inconsistent year to year, and the loose gully rock is a real hazard for parties above/below each other. Expect 1 rappel as the norm on this route (occasionally a short second one depending on exact line through the middle/north notch), well short of full pitch length.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward on the lower pitches by rappelling/downclimbing back toward the talus cone from natural (tree) anchors. Once committed across the crux traverse pitch, it is generally easier to continue to the tree-rappel/gully descent on the east side than to reverse the exposed traverse.

pitch_detail.notes: Roughly 300 ft of low-quality, low-angle slab/4th-5th class terrain leading to the 'Lunch Ledge' belay.

The route's namesake pitch and best rock; climb ~5.8 moves out right, protected by old fixed pitons. Since a Nov 2021 rockfall, the far end now involves an unprotected 5.9-10- downclimb — verify current condition before committing.
Downclimb off the far end of the traverse to a 4th-class ramp, then ascend the ramp toward the summit approach; many parties bypass the loose, exposed true-summit ridge.

approach_variants.name: Talus cone below the west face
approach_variants.notes:
The west face rises above the houses on the Alpental access road. Every road along it carrying a 'Strasse' name is private, and the Alpental Community Club has since 2021 prohibited both driving and walking on them; climbers report being confronted. The talus cone under the face therefore has to be reached by a line that does not cross private land, and there is no established or signed path to it — this is the part of the approach with no fixed answer.

Once on the talus, make a rising traverse up toward the far left (north) end of the west face's talus field. At the top end of the field there is a rocky stream bed, which may be dry depending on the season; that streambed marks the north end of the talus and is the last realistic water.

Wear a helmet on the talus. Climber-triggered rockfall here is a real hazard, from your own party as much as from anyone above.
hazards: no established approach to the talus - the direct approach crosses private roads that residents forbid, and climbers have been confronted

approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the top of the talus cone you scramble a couple of hundred feet of loose, mossy, dirty slab before any roped climbing. That dirty scrambling is part of the approach, not the route — the base of the climb is where it ends against the face proper.

The first pitch wanders about 100 ft of low fourth to low fifth class to a TREE belay. The tree is the confirmation. If you are 100 ft up and there is nothing to belay off, you are not on the line.

Negative marker: the rocky, usually dry streambed marks the far NORTH end of the talus field. If you are south of it and the wall above you is short and clean with bolts on it, you have drifted round to the sport climbing at the base of Guye's south wall and are on a different aspect of the mountain.

Apart from the traverse pitch higher up, the rock on this face is generally poor and loose. Loose rock low down is normal here and is not evidence you are off route.

The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.

bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

backups.name: North Face
backups.fa: Dallas Kloke and Bryce Simon, July 1976. First winter ascent (to the summit ridge): Stuart Taylor and Ade Miller, March 13, 2005
gear: Slings and tat for improvised anchors
Bivouac kit for a camp at 4,000 ft
hazards: Large, sometimes loose chockstones in the summit gully.
A serious, committing alpine rock route on one of the biggest, least-documented walls in the North Cascades.
backups.overview: A serious, rarely-repeated alpine rock route up Davis Peak's huge north-facing cirque wall: four pitches up a prominent central chimney system, then three pitches out onto an exposed rib of delicate face climbing, finishing through a gully choked with large chockstones to the summit.
backups.beta: First climbed by Andy Cairns and Bryan Burdo (Affiliated Climbers of the Montlake Erratic). The route climbs the northern cirque via a central chimney system — possibly a melted-out variant of an earlier 1974 Kloke-Simon line — for four pitches, then exits left onto an exposed rib for three pitches of delicate face climbing, before re-entering a gully with large ('monstrous') chockstones leading to the summit. Part of the first ascent was done by moonlight.
backups.turnaround: Make the decision on the mid-face snowfield, before you commit to the crux pitches. Ask whether you can be established above the chockstone with enough daylight left to climb the upper couloir AND get the top 1,500 ft of the 6,000-ft south-side descent done in the light. If the answer is no, go back down to the glacier while downclimbing is still an option. Two things worsen steadily through the day and neither is negotiable: the cornices over the couloir, and the south-facing descent snow, which the 2005 party found already turned to mush by the sun in mid-March. Getting into the timber after dark is what turns this climb into an epic.
backups.rappels: No fixed anchors and no established rappel line. The rock is compact enough that the 2005 party wrote that 'rap anchors aren't going to be leaping out at you' — retreating from mid-face means leaving pins. On topping out they rappelled from pitons off the top of the couloir onto the SE ridge and then walked the south side down. Carry a pin rack and tat if you want the option of going back down the face.
backups.face: Northeast Face — the 5,250-ft wall above Stetattle Creek
backups.comms: Assume no coverage. Both trailheads sit deep in the Skagit River gorge below the Gorge and Diablo dams, and the climb itself is on a north-facing wall boxed in by Sourdough Mountain and the Pickets; North Cascades National Park advises that cellular service is limited or absent through its backcountry. A satellite messenger or PLB is the practical option. Seattle City Light's Newhalem and Diablo company towns are the nearest places to raise help by telephone, and the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount is the nearest staffed park facility. Note that the timber on the descent is dense enough that the 2005 party could not even see the lights of the dam from it.
backups.descent: Over the top and down the far side: rappel from the top of the couloir onto the SE ridge, then descend the entire south slope roughly 6,000 ft to the Gorge Creek bridge on SR 20. Do not plan on reversing the face.

waypoints.name: Stetattle Creek Trailhead, Diablo (approach; currently closed by fire damage)
Gorge Creek bridge, SR 20 (~MP 122) — descent exit and shuttle car

timing.recommendedStart: Leave the road at first light on the approach day so you reach the glacier-toe bivouac with time to look at the face; start up the glacier at first light on the climbing day so the couloir is done and the south-side descent begun before afternoon sun softens everything.

backups.detailed_rack: Directly from the 2005 gear notes: a full set of wires, knifeblades, lost arrows, and Friends/cams from #1 to #3.5, plus 'a picket might have been nice.' Add a few short and medium ice screws — stubbies specifically, since the useful placements were in thin ice under an overhang and in the ice above the chockstone — a single rope, two technical ice tools and crampons. The pitons are not optional: the rock is compact and the party wrote that they were later 'very glad of the knifeblades' on the runout bulge below the chockstone. Belays were improvised from a cam, a stubby screw and a doubtful horn. Bring slings and tat for rappel anchors you may have to leave behind.
what_to_bring: Compass and USGS 7.5' Diablo Dam quad — the descent timber is too thick to see the dam lights, and a bearing error puts you back in Stetattle Creek
Headlamp with spare batteries; the 2005 party credited a bright headlamp with saving them repeatedly
Altimeter or GPS — Beckey's stated couloir-top elevation is wrong by roughly 500 ft
Footwear or a plan for the Stetattle Creek ford
Water carry for the south-side descent, which is dry
Satellite messenger or PLB
Light bivouac gear, stove and no-cook backup
North Cascades wilderness permit for the overnight
Shuttle-car keys — the climb finishes four road miles from the approach trailhead
pro_tips: This is a rarely-repeated, serious objective on one of the biggest walls in the North Cascades; modern route-finding beta is thin, so treat any description (including this one) as provisional.
watch_out: The chimney system may follow (in a melted-out form) an earlier 1974 Kloke-Simon line, per the first-ascent report — expect variable/unconfirmed conditions on a rarely-repeated route.
Chockstones in the final gully are described as 'monstrous' — test them before committing weight.
backups.pro_needs: Poor to marginal throughout. The lower band is compact gneiss and was simul-climbed with long gaps between pieces; the crux traverse across a partially iced slab was described as terrain where 'falling would not be good, so he thoughtfully doesn't'. Pins are the primary protection. The one properly protected move on the route is the chockstone itself — a cam below the roof and a stubby screw in the good ice on the left. On the upper couloir and rib, expect simul-climbing with occasional gear and very large exposure. Nothing about this route rewards a cam-only rack.
backups.best_season: Both ends of the calendar have been used. The first ascent was in July, so the line goes as a summer rock-and-snow route; the only recorded winter ascent was 13 March 2005. Late winter through early spring is the more attractive window: the couloir is filled and frozen, the lower rock band takes hooks, thin ice and turf instead of being bare compact slab, the bergschrund is filled in, and the slide alder on the approach has no foliage. Against that, the snowpack must be settled — the whole route sits under the summit cornices — and the Stetattle Creek ford is unpleasant in any month. Consult the NWAC West Slopes North forecast before committing. Note that the approach trail is presently closed by fire damage regardless of season.
backups.approach: Approached via Davis Peak's northern cirque, gained from the Gorge Creek/Stetattle Creek drainages north of the peak; beyond that the first-ascent account gives no detailed trailhead-to-base mileage.
backups.descent_text:
The 2005 party's words: 'Stuart doesn't fancy descending to the river any more than I do. So, one way or another; we're going down the other side.' That is the correct call — the northeast face has no easy retreat, and the south side, though long and unpleasant, is walkable.

From the top of the couloir at about 6,700 ft, rappel from pitons onto the SE ridge (or continue up the ridge to the 7,054 ft summit first if the clock allows). Descend the south side following the South Slope and Ridge route in reverse: down the ridge crest, past the 5,720+ ft saddle, over or around Point 5872, and then straight down the sustained trackless forest of the south slope to the highway.

The key is daylight. The 2005 party got the upper 1,500 ft done in the light and credit that with saving them; it let them avoid all the cliff bands and the rappelling-off-trees that comes with getting them wrong. They reached the top of the timber just after dark, found the forest thick but not as bad as feared — no cliffs and not much slide alder on their line — and took four hours from there to the road. The timber is dense enough that they never saw the lights from the dam the whole way down; the only lights they saw were a car's, a few hundred feet above the highway. A bit of compass work is what kept them from ending up back in Stetattle Creek.

You finish at the Gorge Creek bridge, about four highway miles from where you parked in Diablo. Arrange a shuttle car — retrieving the truck cost the 2005 party another half hour on foot at the end of a two-day climb.
backups.bail: There is no good bail from the northeast face. Below the mid-face snowfield you can reverse the approach pitches (they were simul-climbed, so this means downclimbing runout terrain) and walk back down the glacier to the bivouac. Once you are traversing the snowfield toward the couloir entrance, retreat means building rappel anchors in compact gneiss that gives up almost nothing — expect to leave a pin rack. Above the chockstone, 'up' is unambiguously the answer; the route tops out on a walkable, if very long, descent side. Treat the mid-face snowfield as the last honest decision point. If you bail from the bivouac instead, reverse the rib and the ford back to the Stetattle Creek trail.

pitch_detail.notes: Four pitches up the prominent central chimney splitting the north face.
Exit left onto an exposed rib for three pitches of delicate face climbing, then a gully with large chockstones to the summit.

backups.itinerary:
Two days, one bivouac. Day 1: sleep near Diablo (there is a 'No Camping' sign the 2005 party parked next to; the legal option is a permitted backcountry site or a night in the Newhalem campground). Leave at first light, hike the Stetattle Creek trail about 2 mi / 3 km, drop 200 ft to ford the creek opposite Davis, then bushwhack and scramble the 3rd/4th-class rib — roping up for the slabby sections — through a slide-alder band above the cliffs to a bivouac on flat snow at the toe of the glacier, 4,000 ft. The 2005 party had bivy coffins dug and a brew on by late afternoon, roughly eight or nine hours from the road, with running water at the site. Spend the evening looking at the face and deciding whether the couloir will go.

Day 2: up the glacier at first light, gear up at the bergschrund, climb the lower band, the snowfield, the crux pitches and the upper couloir to the summit ridge near 6,700 ft. Tag the summit if you have time. Then commit to the full south-side descent — 6,000 ft — aiming to be below the cliff bands before dark, and walk or shuttle the four road miles back to Diablo.

road.name: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway)
road.status: Paved and open year-round as far as Newhalem, Gorge Creek and Diablo; plowed to the seasonal gate. Approach parking for this route is at the Diablo townsite, milepost 126.
road.driveNote: Turn into Diablo at milepost 126. Older directions run you to the northernmost street and across a lawn to find the unmarked Stetattle Creek trail on the east bank of the creek; this is a quiet residential neighbourhood, so bypass the houses and drive the lakeshore past the powerhouse to the large public parking lot with restrooms built for the Seattle City Light dam tours, and walk the extra distance. Since the climb finishes at the Gorge Creek bridge at about milepost 122, leave a shuttle car there.
road.seasonalGate: WSDOT closes SR 20 for the winter between milepost 134 (Ross Dam Trailhead) and milepost 171 (Silver Star gate), moving the gates down to milepost 120 (Newhalem) and milepost 178 (Early Winters) in deep winter conditions. Both Davis Peak access points are normally west of the gate and reachable year-round, but check WSDOT before a winter attempt — in 2026 the section between milepost 130 and milepost 156 stayed shut well past the usual reopening because of major storm damage.

climate.fall: Cool, dry and often stable in a good year, but the couloir is at its most stripped and the days are short for a two-day climb finishing with a 6,000-ft forest descent.
climate.spring: The most attractive window for the face. Late winter and early spring keep the couloir filled and frozen, the lower rock band icy rather than bare slab, the bergschrund closed, and the slide alder on the approach rib leafless. Watch for wet-loose and wet-slab release on the sun-hit south-facing descent by early afternoon.
climate.summer: The couloir loses its ice; the first ascent went in July, so the line still goes as a rock-and-snow route at mid-fifth class on the lower band. The south-side descent becomes an oven and its water sources dry up, and the approach brush is at full leaf.
climate.winter: Ascents have been made. The one recorded winter ascent was 13 March 2005; a party on the south side climbed in January and recorded -22F at the 5,720-ft saddle. Expect deep snow, very large cornices along the summit ridge, and daylight that is the limiting factor on the descent.
climate.typical: West-side maritime North Cascades. Pacific fronts drive heavy orographic precipitation onto these slopes, giving deep winter snow and significant rain in the other seasons. The base of the mountain is only about 1,100 ft above sea level while the summit is 7,054 ft, so the snowline moves through nearly 6,000 ft of relief and conditions on the approach can be completely different from conditions on the face.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North (avalanche); NOAA/NWS Seattle point forecast for the Diablo Dam quadrangle

emergency.notes: Leave an itinerary with someone and be specific about which Davis Peak you mean — there is another one near Cle Elum, and the two are 90 miles apart. Because you approach from Diablo (MP 126) and descend to Gorge Creek (MP 122), a shuttle car left at the wrong end is itself a hazard. There is no cell coverage; carry a satellite messenger. Your permit itinerary is the record rangers will work from.
emergency.county: Whatcom County, Washington. The peak and both access points lie inside the North Cascades National Park Complex, so the National Park Service leads search and rescue.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Road, Marblemount WA 98267 — 360-854-7245 (park main line 360-854-7200). Open roughly mid-May to mid-October; in the off-season contact the park headquarters in Sedro-Woolley.
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, 2000 Hospital Dr, Sedro-Woolley WA 98284 — 360-856-6021, 24-hour emergency department. It is well down SR 20 to the west of Newhalem.
